text: Rational Electrolyte Solvent Screening for Practical Lithium−Sulfur Batteries Lin Peng,# Lishan Lin,# Zitao Feng, Xiaoxian Guan, Jingwen Lai, Yang Xiao, Luyi Chen,* Yuepeng Cai,* and Qifeng Zheng* Cite This: ACS Energy Lett. 2026, 11, 4125−4135 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: Practical lithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries demand rapid sulfur redox kinetics and high Li-metal compatibility simultaneously, which cannot achieve this objective using current electrolyte based on 1,2-dimethoxyethane and 1,3-dioxolane.
Herein, we propose a solvent screening criterion using the dielectric constant (εr) and donor number (DN) as a synergistic descriptor.
Guided by this εr−DN screening criterion, 75 solvents were classified as strong, midstrong, middle, weak, and nonsolvation solvents, respectively.

The combination of midstrong/ weak solvation solvents endows a distinctly gradient lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) solvation structure, suppressing their shuttle effect and enhancing Li-metal compatibility.
This bestows the Li−S coin cell with an extremely high areal capacity of 9.4 mAh cm−2 under a high S mass loading (8.6 mg cm−2) and a low E/S ratio (3.6 μL mg−1).
As a proof-of-concept, a 3 Ah-level pouch cell delivers a high energy density of 369 Wh kg−1.

L ithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries, featuring an ultrahigh theoretical energy density (up to 2600 Wh kg−1) and low cost, abundant S as the cathode material, are considered as the leading candidates for next-generation energy storage systems.1,2 However, their industrialization has been persistently hindered by critical challenges, among which electrolyte design and optimization play a pivotal role.3 The electrolyte serves as not only an ion-transport medium but also a core component, which profoundly governs the dissolution, diffusion, and conversion of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) and critically impacts the stability of electrode−electrolyte interfaces.4 Benefiting from the prior lithium-ion battery technology, early research predominantly employed ether-based solvents, such as 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) as the baseline electrolytes.5,6 Although ether solvents exhibit high solubility for LiPSs, which ensures favorable sulfur conversion kinetics, this property also causes the shuttle effect of LiPSs.7,8 Dissolved LiPSs species migrate between the cathode and anode, causing irreversible active material rapid loss and lithium metal anode (LMA) corrosion.9,10 Recently, various electrolyte strategies have been explored to suppress the shuttle effect of LiPSs.11,12 For instance, employing weak-solvating-power solvents, e.g., carbonates,13 single-oxygen ether,14 and hydrofluorinated ether,15 results in incomplete sulfur redox reactions and easy formation of passivation layer on the cathode surface.

Introducing ionic liquids or highly concentrated electrolytes effectively restricted LiPSs dissolution, however also leads to high viscosity, low ionic conductivity, and high costs.16,17 Although these approaches have achieved incremental progress, they often inevitably face a dilemma of trade-offs: suppressing shuttle effect of LiPSs comes at the expense of compromised conversion kinetics or interfacial stability.18 Then, to achieve a high S utilization under lean electrolyte condition, a series of Gutmann’s donor number (DN) solvents with strong-solvating-power are proposed to boost the solubility of LiPSs leading to a rapid conversion kinetics based on a solid−liquid−solid S redox process.19,20 From the perspective of electrolyte engineering, a fundamental understanding of the LiPSs’ solvation is essential for the industrialization of Li−S batteries.

Further, in designing new electrolyte systems, the reliance on the empirical trial-and-error approaches and the lack of comprehensive theoretical guidance are the primarily reasons of the puzzling relationship between screening solvents and the solvation of LiPSs.21−23 Recently, several key parameters with great potential have recently been proposed to understand this relationship, as following: (i) The Gutmann’s DN of a solvent dictates Li+ coordination strength: high DN solvents dissolve Received: March 16, 2026 Revised: April 14, 2026 Accepted: April 17, 2026 Published: April 24, 2026 Letter http://pubs.acs.org/journal/aelccp © 2026 American Chemical Society 4125 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.6c00790 ACS Energy Lett. 2026, 11, 4125−4135 Downloaded from pubs.​acs.​org/​aelccp/​article-pdf/​11/​5/​4125/​64809067/​nz6c00790.​pdf by TSINGHUA UNIV user on 24 September 2026

LiPSs but exacerbate their shuttle effect, while low DN solvents suppress dissolution at the expense of S conversion kinetics.24 (ii) The Gutmann’s acceptor number (AN) indicates Lewis acidity of a solvent.
High AN solvents, due to their stronger electrophilic properties, interact strongly with polysulfide anions (high solvation energy), which risk parasitic reactions.

Whereas low AN solvents facilitate robust solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation on the anode.25,26 (iii) Relative permittivity (εr), also known as the dielectric constant, indicates how readily a solvent molecule can be aligned by an electric field.

High εr solvents can modulate the solvation of LiPSs, dissociating them into free ions but accelerating diffusion.27,28 In contrast, low εr solvents restrict LiPSs diffusion by forming contact ion pairs or aggregates, yet impairing redox activity.28 However, aside from the ion−solvent interactions, quantitative models for solvent− solvent and LiPSs−solvent interactions are poorly understood, particularly in binary solvent electrolyte systems.
Therefore, it is imperative to bridge the fundamental gap between the nanoscopic screening criteria and macroscopic electrochemical performance.

Herein, we propose an electrolyte solvent screening criterion based on εr and DN, where 75 electrolyte solvents were classified and evaluated by using seven critical electrochemical performance parameters.

These seven parameters are polarization voltage, cycle life of Li||Li symmetric cells, LiPSs shuttle current, Li2S nucleation overpotential and deposition capacity, and average capacity and average CE of Li−S coin cells.

The electrolyte formula combining midstrong solvation (2,5- dimethyl-1,2,5-thiadiazolidin 1-oxide, CSA) and weak solvation (2-methyltetrahydrofuran, MeTHF) solvents outperforms all other electrolyte formulations.

The Li−S coin cell employing CSA/MeTHF electrolyte achieves an initial areal capacity of 9.4 mAh cm−2 at a high S loading of 8.6 mg cm−2 and low E/S of 3.6 μL mg−1.
Furthermore, the effectiveness of this midstrong and weak solvent combination is also examined in 3 Ah level pouch cell.
According to the Born−Haber cycle (Figure 1a), the dissolution of a Li salt in a solvent requires a negative Gibbs free energy change (ΔG = ΔH −TΔS < 0).
This is a thermodynamic prerequisite for forming a homogeneous and stable electrolyte system.
The dissociation of a crystalline Li salt first involves its endothermic ionization into anions and cations, which is a process primarily governed by the lattice energy (ΔUlat).
Then, the dissociated ions are solvated by solvent molecules, forming a coordination structure in an exothermic process dominated by the solvation enthalpy (ΔHsol).

Electrolytes in Li−S batteries, which typically operate via a solid−liquid−solid conversion mechanism, usually contain three main Li salts: lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), LiNO3, and LiPSs (Figure 1b).
Using Li2S6 as a representative LiPSs, its dissolution and precipitation are correlated with the solvation structure and the conversion equilibrium.
Specifically, the solvation structure of LiPSs can be modulated by high εr solvent with enhancement of a strong electrostatic shielding effect for ions.
This leads to more free ions with increased entropy (Figure 1c) and favors the dissociation of LiPSs.

Moreover, based on the theory of Lewis acids and bases, the coordination environment of Li+ can be regulated with high DN solvent, resulting in lower solvation enthalpy change (ΔHsol; Figure 1d; further discussion is provided in Supplementary Note 2.1).29 Further, the dual-descriptor, namely, εr and DN, was proposed to classify the 75 organic solvents in Figures 1e and S1, and Tables S1−8.

Region I (0 ≤DN < 19 kcal mol−1 and 20 ≤εr < 100), including most carbonate solvents, shows ultralow solubility for LiNO3.26,28 Due to the high DN value of NO3 − (22.2 kcal mol−1), most carbonate solvents provide an insufficient solvation enthalpy (ΔHsol) to overcome the lattice energy (ΔUlat) of LiNO3.

Unfortunately, these solvents exhibit high reactivity toward LiPSs via nucleophilic attack, resulting in rapid active material loss and severe side reactions at the cathode (Figures S2−S4 and Supplementary Note S2.2).30 Region II (25 ≤DN < 40 kcal mol−1 and 1 ≤εr < 20) contains polar protic nitrogenous solvents, which may undergo deprotonation Figure 2.

Thus, the screening criteria based on DN and εr, coupled with thermodynamic analysis of solute dissolution processes, provide a basic framework for designing rational electrolytes in Li−S batteries.

In this work, five representative solvents were selected to design binary solvent electrolyte formulations (Figure 2a and Table S9): dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) from Region S, 2,5- dimethyl-1,2,5-thiadiazolidin 1-oxide (CSA) from Region M-S, 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) from Region M, 2-methyltetrahydrofuran (MeTHF) from Region W, and 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE) from Region N.
CSA was synthesized via a nucleophilic substitution reaction (Figure S6) and confirmed by 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy (Figures S7 and S8).

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that calculated the lowest negative electrostatic potential (i.e., ESPmin) of the five solvents follows the strength trend: DMSO > CSA > DME > MeTHF > TTE (Figure S9), indicating a reduced trend in solvation capability.
Further, the electrolyte was prepared using an optimal molar ratio of LiTFSI:CSA:MeTHF = 1:4:6, with the detailed optimization shown in Figures S10 and S11.
Using this formulation, Li||Li2S6 cell exhibits a capacity retention of 93% after 60 cycles with high average CE of 99.4% (Figure S12).
All other formulas were prepared with an optimal molar ratio of LiTFSI: solvent 1: solvent 2: LiNO3 = 1:4:6:0.2, as detailed in Table S10.
Due to the insolubility of LiNO3 in hydrofluoroether solvents, LiNO3 was omitted from the TTE-containing electrolyte formulations.
Additionally, a conventional electrolyte of 1 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiNO3 in DME:DOL (1:1 by volume; denoted as DD) was employed as the reference electrolyte.
The density, viscosity, and ionic conductivity of these electrolytes were measured and are summarized in Table S11.
Li+ solvation structures in all electrolyte systems were investigated by using Raman spectroscopy (Figure S13).

Characteristic peak shift in the binary solvent electrolyte systems reveal a consistent solvation strength trend (DMSO > CSA > DME > MeTHF > TTE), confirming the reliability of solvent selection criteria.
In the DMSO/CSA (S/M-S) electrolyte, the C−S−C stretching vibration of DMSO exhibits a significant blue shift, indicating strong coordination between DMSO and Li+ (Figure S13a).
Meanwhile, the N−S−N stretching vibration of CSA shows a slight blue shift, indicating partial coordination between CSA and Li+.
This suggests a competitively coordinated Li+ solvation structure in DMSO/ CSA.
Similar competitive coordination was observed in CSA/ DME (M-S/M), DME/MeTHF (M/W), and DME/DOL (DD) (Figure S13b−d).

In contrast, DMSO/DME (S/M), DMSO/MeTHF (S/W), CSA/MeTHF (M-S/W), DMSO/ TTE (S/N), CSA/TTE (M-S/N), DME/TTE (M/N), and MeTHF/TTE (W/N) exhibit a different Li+ solvation structure (Figures S14 and S15), which features only one coordinated solvent and another free solvent (noncoordinated).
This confirms that, besides coordination capability of a single solvent, the combination of two solvents is another key factor for binary solvent electrolytes to regulate the Li+ solvation structure.

First, the LMA compatibility with each electrolyte formula was evaluated by Li||Li symmetric cells, whose polarization voltage could reflect the kinetics during the Li deposition and stripping process.

Both polarization voltage and cycle life of Li|| Li symmetric cells using various electrolytes were selected as the primary two screening parameters for the binary solvent electrolytes, which was evaluated using Li||Li symmetric cells cycled at 0.5 mA cm−2 and 0.5 mAh cm−2 (Figures 2b, S16, and S17).

Only the M-S/W, M/W, M/N, W/N, and DD electrolytes simultaneously met the demands of polarization voltage below 50 mV and cycle life exceeding 800 h, demonstrating the excellent compatibility with LMA.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of cycled LMAs, using M-S/W, M/W, M/ N, W/N, and DD electrolytes, revealed a clear morphologyperformance correlation of small polarization voltages, long cycle life, and smooth morphologies.

In contrast, those that induced large polarization voltages and short cycle life, using S/ M-S, S/W, S/M, S/N, M-S/M, and M-S/N electrolytes, resulted in cracked, porous, mossy deposited morphologies.
These results can be attributed to the distinct solvent properties: (1) DMSO with strong solvation ability accompanies intrinsic corrosion, leading to short cycle life.
(2) CSA, with midstrong solvation ability, offers a balance between strong donor ability and compatibility toward Li metal.
(3) TTE, as a nonsolvation solvent, contributes to low ionic conductivity and high viscosity, which could aggravate Li dendritic growth.

Given that the multispecies and multiphase of LiPSs in Li−S batteries, their shuttle current (SC) is adopted as the third key screening parameter, which directly reflects the loss of active materials induced by the corrosion reaction between LiPSs and LMA.11 The SC of LiPSs was measured via potentiostatic tests between 2.2 and 2.9 V (Figure S18).

Previously reported work has demonstrated that an antisolvent-derived encapsulation solvation structure can effectively suppress the LiPS shuttle.32,33 In this work, only S/N, M-S/W, M-S/N, M/N, and W/N electrolytes show an average SC below 10 μA cm−2 based on Li|| Li2S6 coin cells (Figure 2c).

Thanks to the solid−liquid−solid conversion mechanism in the S cathode, both nucleation overpotential (ΔVnuc) and deposition capacity of lithium sulfide (Li2S) are critical ratedetermining steps,34 representing the energy barriers for Li2S nucleation and growth.
Consequently, both ΔVnuc and Li2S deposition capacities from Li−S coin cells were used as the following two key screening parameters for these electrolytes.
As shown in Figures 2d, S19, and S20, only S/M, M-S/M, and M-S/ W simultaneously met the demand of ΔVnuc below 30 mV and a Li2S deposition capacity exceeding 600 mAh g−1.
This implies that enhanced solvation capability effectively accelerates the conversion kinetics of sulfur species.
Moreover, average discharge capacity and average CE over 100 cycles were proposed as the last two key parameters for assessing practicality.

As shown in Figures 2e, S19, and S20, only the M-S/W electrolyte achieved an average discharge capacity exceeding 900 mAh g−1 and an average CE of 99.9% over 100 cycles at 0.2 C, indicating high S utilization and excellent cycling stability.

and deposition capacity of Li2S, and (4) average capacity and average CE (Figure 2f and Table S12).
The conventional DD electrolyte, with moderate LiPSs solubility, exhibits a typical solid−liquid−solid conversion process (Figure S21).

This process prior forms a twodimensional (2D) Li2S deposition morphology, leading to low S utilization and significant corrosion with LMA.35 Coupling a strong solvating solvent with LiPSs could regulate the LiPSs solvation structure, promote a three-dimensional (3D) Li2S deposition morphology, and provide an additional conversion pathway.

However, this approach often exacerbates LiPSs corrosion with LMA.36 Conversely, employing a solvent with a low LiPSs solubility can create a sparingly solvated structure that mitigates LMA corrosion.

Yet, this strategy also results in 2D Li2S deposition and sluggish conversion kinetics.37 Given the critical role of the LiPSs solvation structure, we further explored the solvent−solvent interactions in the M-S/W electrolyte to elucidate the underlying structure−property relationships in this binary solvent electrolyte.
The solubility of LiPSs was investigated in Figure S22.
Ten mM Li2Sx (x = 2, 4, 6, 8) in CSA:MeTHF (4:6 by molar) exhibits uniform a darkbrown color, indicating high LiPSs dissolubility.
In contrast, 10 mM Li2Sx in DME:DOL (1:1 by vol.) shows visible precipitate (the dotted box), indicating poor dissociation and low dissolubility of polysulfides (Sx 2−) species.
The ionic conductivity of 0.1 M Li2Sx in CSA:MeTHF is higher than that in DME:DOL (Figure S23).
This enhanced Li+ solvation and promoted Li2Sx dissociation could be attributable to CSA with high εr and DN.
The sulfur atomic concentration ([S]) in a saturated Li2S6/CSA solution reaches approximately 18 mol L−1, which is significantly higher than that in DME (9 mol L−1; Figure S24).

Conversely, [S] in a saturated Li2S6/MeTHF solution is only 0.6 mol L−1, lower than that in DOL (1.0 mol L−1). 17O NMR spectroscopy was employed to characterize the LiPSs solvation structure (Figure 3a−d).
The 17O chemical shift of 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA exhibits a significant upfield shift of −0.16 ppm, whereas that of 0.1 M Li2S6 in DME shows a smaller upfield shift (−0.11 ppm).
This difference confirms a stronger coordination between CSA and Li+ than with DME, resulting in a CSA-dominated Li2S6 solvation structure.
The 17O chemical shifts of 0.1 M Li2S6 in DOL and MeTHF exhibit slight upfield shifts (−0.03 and −0.01 ppm, respectively), indicating weak coordination with Li+.

This suggests that MeTHF is mostly located in the outer shell of Li2S6 solvation structure, forming a gradient distribution of mixed solvents. 0.1 M Li2S6 in the mixed solvents (CSA:MeTHF and DME:DOL) were further analyzed by comparative 7Li NMR spectroscopy (Figure 3e).
The shield effect of Li+ in CSA:MeTHF is stronger than in DME:DOL due to the stronger coordination capability of CSA compared to DME.
This verifies the efficacy of CSA:MeTHF in regulating the LiPSs solvation structure.
Furthermore, the solvation structure of LiPSs was observed by using molecular dynamics (MD) simulation.
To simulate the local environment around LiPSs in Li−S batteries, 0.2 M Li2S6 was introduced into the electrolyte of 1.0 M LiTFSI in CSA:MeTHF and DME:DOL, respectively.

From the result of radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure S25a, the S6 2− exhibits a strong correlation peak with both Li+ and CSA within 4.5 Å in 0.2 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in CSA:MeTHF solution, indicating that CSA occupies the inner solvation sheath of Li2S6.

Furthermore, the coordination number result in Figure S25c reveals that CSA exhibits a preferential increase around 3.2 Å, while MeTHF shows extremely slow growth within 5.0 Å, also confirming the gradient solvation structure of LiPSs.
In contrast, for 0.2 M Li2S6 + 1.0 M LiTFSI in DME:DOL solution, both DME and DOL occupy the solvation shell of S6 2−(Figures S25b−d).
Furthermore, 1H−1H correlation spectroscopy (COSY) was conducted to elucidate the solvent−solvent interaction in the LiPSs solvation structure.
In the COSY spectra (Figure 3f,g), both the abscissa and ordinate represent the 1H NMR chemical shifts.

The off-diagonal cross-peaks arise through 1H−1H coupling between protons, which occurs through chemical bonds and provides information about intramolecular connectivity.38 Diagonal signals typically represent intramolecular interactions, while off-diagonal cross-peaks can indicate either intramolecular (through-space) or intermolecular correlations.
For 0.1 M Li2S6 in DME:DOL, only diagonal signals corresponding to intramolecular interactions were observed, indicating no detectable 1H−1H coupling.
Remarkably, 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF shows clear off-diagonal cross-peaks, signifying intermolecular 1H−1H (a, d) coupling in Figure 3h.
This result provides clear evidence of a specific CSA−MeTHF interaction, which is conducive to regulating the LiPSs solvation structure.

Additionally, 7Li NMR diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (DOSY) was employed to analyze the diffusion process of Li+ in LiPSs solutions.39 As shown in Figure S26, 2D DOSY results display well-resolved 7Li chemical shift signals.
Notably, 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF exhibits a diffusion rate of Li+ (DLi +, sol.) of 3.1 × 10−10 m2 s−1, which is less than a half value measured in DME:DOL (6.3 × 10−10 m2 s−1).

Thanks to the critical role of the LiPSs aggregation during the S-based solid−liquid−solid conversion mechanism,40 the solvated radii of LiPSs in electrolyte was further measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS).
As shown in Figure S27, 0.1 M Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF exhibits a larger solvated radius (7.5 nm) than that in DME:DOL (4.2 nm).
This suggests a greater degree of aggregation occurs in the CSA:MeTHF electrolyte.

In addition to suppressing the LiPSs shuttle effect and stabilizing LMA by reducing parasitic reactions, we assume that the intrinsic CSA− MeTHF interaction triggers the formation of Li2S6 clusters, which also affect the reaction kinetics to promote 3D Li2S deposition.41,42 The viscosity of 0.1 M Li2S6 was measured to calculate the diffusion rate of Li2S6 (DLi2S6) using Einstein- Stokes eq (Figure 3i).43 Li2S6 in CSA:MeTHF shows a DLi2S6 of 2.3 × 10−11 m2 s−1, which is lower than that in DME:DOL (8.9 × 10−11 m2 s−1), confirming a slower diffusion process of Li2S6.
Thus, the CSA−MeTHF interaction enables the electrolyte to form not only a gradient solvation structure but also clustered LiPSs.

The solid−liquid−solid conversion in Li−S batteries involves a unique multistep, multielectron, multispecies, and multiphase (termed as “4M”) conversion redox process.
Within this process, Li2S deposition behavior and its conversion kinetics are critical for achieving a high S utilization and long-term cycling stability.
To investigate this, Li2S deposition and dissolution experiments were conducted using both electrolytes, with the results shown in Figures S28−S32.
These results confirm that the primary inner solvation sheath of the CSA/MeTHF electrolyte enables the formation of a three-dimensional (3D) Li2S deposit.

Additionally, cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests at various scan rates demonstrate that CSA/MeTHF electrolyte with a gradient LiPSs solvation structure strongly facilitates rapid LiPSs conversion kinetics (Figures S33−S37).
Then, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted to evaluate the dynamic interfacial chemistry of the S cathode.
Li||Li2S6 coin cell with a S loading (MS) of 1.4 mg cm−2 was assembled and tested at 0.1 C.
As shown in Figures 4a−c, at the initial states-of-charge (SoC) (i), high-order LiPSs dissolve in the CSA/MeTHF electrolyte, leading to a smooth surface of CF with low impedance.
At SoC (ii), where high-order LiPSs transform into low-order species, tiny Li2S particles begin to gradually electrodeposit on the CF surface with a slightly increased impedance.
The Li2S particle becomes nonuniform at SoC (iii), showing higher impedance than that at SoC (ii).
At SoC (iv), an island-like Li2S morphology forms.
The abundant triple-phase interface among Li2S, the CF substrate, and the electrolyte facilitates efficient Li+ transport and diffusion.
During the discharge process, the Li2S particles become small with low electrical impedances at the SoC (v), resulting from the oxidation of Li2S to LiPSs.
At SoC (vi), Li2S is fully converted to S, resulting in a smooth film with white insulating regions on the CF surface.
This morphology indicates a highly reversible conversion process.
From the EIS result in Figures S38a,b, increased impedances are remarkably observed at SoCs iii, iv, and v using DD electrolyte.
This is mainly attributed to the limited LiPSs solubility in DD electrolyte, which induces 2D growth of Li2S with a film-like morphology on the CF surface (Figure S38c).
Further, this premature and compact passivation severely hinders subsequent LiPSs reduction reactions, resulting in low S utilization and sluggish conversion kinetics.
Moreover, the distribution of relaxation times (DRT) method based on the EIS result was conducted to analyze the interfacial evolution during the redox conversion reaction.

As shown in Figures S39 and S40, the DRT profiles acquired at different stages of charge−discharge reveal seven characteristic peaks across high to low frequency range.44 Each peak corresponds to a distinct physical or chemical process with a specific time scale.45 These peaks are assigned as follows: interparticle resistance (P1), double-layer relaxation (P2), solid−electrolyte interphase (P3), positive electrode charge transfer (P4), positive electrode charge transfer (P5), polysulfide diffusion (P6), and general diffusion (P7).
During cycling, the interfacial evolution using CSA/MeTHF electrolyte is primarily governed by P7 peak (canary area), especially at SoC iv (Figure 4d).
In contrast, the cell using DD electrolytes exhibits dominance of both P6 and P7 peaks at SoCs (iii, iv, and v) in Figure 4e.
In addition, XPS and morphological analyses reveal stark differences between the two electrolytes (Figures S41−45).

The CSA/MeTHF electrolyte enables 3D porous Li2S cathode deposition and a smooth LMA surface enriched with protective high-valence sulfur species (SO4 2−/ SO3 2−), demonstrating excellent LMA compatibility.

In sharp contrast, the DD electrolyte produces a compact 2D Li2S film on the cathode and a mossy LMA surface dominated by corrosive low-valence sulfur species (Li2S, Li2S2, and LiPSs), highlighting severe polysulfide-induced LMA degradation.

Understanding the origin of these distinct interfacial chemistries is crucial for advancing fundamental issues of Li− S battery electrochemistry.
The galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) was applied for decoupling the electrochemical polarization during the 4 M conversion reaction.
Electrochemical polarization is defined as the deviation of the electrode potential from its equilibrium value.

The Li||S cells with a lean electrolyte of 4 μL mg−1 and high MS of 4.5 mg cm−2 were subjected to GITT measurements, including galvanostatic discharge or charge at 0.05 C for 20 min and following a relaxation time of 1 h for each GITT step (Figures 4f,g and S46).
Usually, the total polarization voltage (ηtotal) is defined as the gap between the working voltage and the equilibrium voltage.

This can be decoupled into three components: ohmic polarization (ηohm), concentration polarization (ηcon), and activation polarization (ηact).14 The values of ηcon and ηohm + ηact could be distinguished from the GITT profile, while the ηohm value is calculated using Ohm’s law from the EIS result (Figures S47).

The relative contributions of each polarization component at different depths of discharge (DoDs) are shown in Figures 4h and S46c.The contribution of ηohm remains minimal throughout the discharge process, indicating that it is not the dominant factor determining the S-based reduction rate.
After the DoD of 25%, ηact becomes the dominant polarization in the DD electrolyte (Figures S46c and S48), indicating sluggish conversion kinetics governed by interfacial chemistry.
These kinetics are limited not only by the LiPSs maximum concentration but also by the protracted liquid−solid conversion process.
Although, for the CSA/ MeTHF electrolyte, the proportion of ηcon exceeds 50% after the DoD of 25%, all three polarization components maintain consistent trends throughout low voltage plateau.

This demonstrates that CSA/MeTHF electrolyte induces stable interfacial chemistry that sustains rapid concentration-dominated conversion, particularly for the shorter order LiPSs.32 Thus, these results demonstrate a clear correlation between interfacial chemistry and electrochemical polarization during the 4 M conversion process, highlighting the critical role of electrolyte engineering.

To verify the suppressed shuttle effect and boosted conversion kinetics of LiPSs resulting from the gradient solvation structure of the CSA/MeTHF electrolyte, Li−S coin cells were first assembled and tested in Figure 5.

With a MS of 1.1 mg cm−2 and E/S ratio of 16.7 μL mg−1, a Li||S coin cell using CSA/MeTHF electrolyte delivers an initial specific capacity of 1037 mAh g−1 at 0.2 C (Figure 5a), verifying efficient S utilization.
And the capacity retention achieves 70% after 300 cycles, corresponding to a low decay rate of only 0.05% per cycle.
The average CE during cycling reaches 99.8%, indicating effectively suppressed LiPSs shuttle effect.

With an increased MS of 3.0 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 7.4 μL mg−1, the initial capacity using CSA/MeTHF achieves 992 mAh g−1 with a small polarization voltage at the low plateau (ΔElow) of 0.232 V (Figures 5b and S49a).
After 130 cycles, the capacity retention remains at 88% with a high average CE of 99.5% (Figure 5c), while ΔElow shows no obvious change (Figure S49b).
In contrast, using DD electrolyte exhibits a significantly large ΔElow in the first cycle, which sharply increased after 130 cycle (Figure S49c).

Since lean electrolyte and high MS are prerequisites for practical high-energy-density Li−S batteries, the electrochemical performance using CSA/MeTHF electrolyte was further evaluated under harsh condition: an E/S of 4.2 μL mg−1 and a MS of 6.3 mg cm−2 in Figures 5d and S50.
The initial capacity reached 1211 mAh g−1 at 0.05 C, corresponding to an areal capacity of 7.6 mAh cm−2.
After 50 cycles, the capacity is retained at 909 mAh g−1 (a capacity retention of 67%), demonstrating excellent cycling stability using high MS and lean electrolyte conditions.

With a MS of 8.6 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 3.6 μL mg−1, the coin cell using the CSA/MeTHF electrolyte delivers an initial capacity of 1094 mAh g−1 at 0.05 C, corresponding to an areal capacity of 9.4 mAh cm−2 (Figures 5e and S51).
After 30 cycles, the areal capacity remains at 7.7 mAh cm−2, significantly exceeding that of commercial lithium-ion batteries (∼4 mAh cm−2).

The outstanding performance under harsh conditions (MS ≥3 mg cm−2 and E/S ≤8 μL mg−1) demonstrates a competitive advantage over most of reported electrolytes for state-of-the-art Li−S batteries (Figure 5f and Table S13).33,36,41,46−53 Finally, a 3 Ah-level Li−S pouch cell was assembled to validate the practicability of this electrolyte screening approach.
The detailed parameters are shown in Figure S52 and Table S14.

As shown in Figure S53a, the Li−S pouch cell using the CSA/ MeTHF electrolyte shows an initial discharge capacity of 3.12 Ah and an initial energy density of 369 Wh kg−1 at 0.03 C, based on the total mass of the pouch cell.
After 15 cycles, the pouch cell still works, and the energy density is maintained at 307 Wh kg−1 (Figure S53b).
It should be noted that this cycling lifespan of 3 Ah-level Li||S pouch cell is only proof-of-concept.

To validate the screening criteria, a new solvent, 4,4,4- trifluoro-N,N-dimethylbutanamide (TFBA) was synthesized (Figures S54−S57), and paired with DOL, forming a gradient solvation structure (TFBA/DOL) that effectively suppresses the LiPSs shuttle effect (Figures S58 and S59).

The TFBA/DOL electrolyte enables stable Li||Li cycling for over 1000 h and delivers 1051 mAh g−1 at 0.2 C with 92% capacity retention after 100 cycles (Figures S60 and S61), confirming the broad applicability of this screening strategy for Li−S batteries.
In conclusion, we developed a screening methodology comprising 75 solvent classifications based on εr and DN, and electrolyte evaluation using seven critical electrochemical performance parameters.

The CSA/MeTHF electrolyte, combining midstrong and weak solvation solvents, exhibits a distinct solvent−solvent interaction that forms a gradient solvation structure, as evidenced by multiple spectroscopic techniques.
Furthermore, the correlations among Li2S electrodeposition, electrode interfacial chemistry, and LiPSs conversion kinetics are demonstrated.
The Li||S coin cell achieves an initial capacity of 1094 mAh g−1 at 0.05 C with a MS of 8.6 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 3.6 μL of mg−1.
Three Ah-level Li−S pouch cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 3.12 Ah and an initial energy density of 369 Wh kg−1.
Additionally, the TFBA/ DOL electrolyte is designed to validate the universality of this screening criterion engineering.

Ltd. 1.2 Synthesis of solvents 2,5-Dimethyl-1,2,5-thiadiazolidine 1-oxide (CSA).

Firstly, anhydrous THF (120 mL), TEA (12 mL), and DMEDA (5.4 mL) were added to the round bottom flask, and the mixture was cooled to −78°C using a liquid nitrogen/acetone cold bath under N2 atmosphere.
Then, SOCl2 (3.6 mL) was added dropwise, and the reaction was stirred for 1 h.
Afterwards, the mixture was maintained at room temperature for 10 h.
The crude mixture was washed with anhydrous THF.

Supplementary notes 2.1 Thermodynamic analysis of the dissolution process The dissolution of solutes (e.g., lithium salts) in solvents is governed by the second law of thermodynamics.
The thermodynamic requirement for spontaneous dissolution is a negative change in Gibbs free energy (ΔG < 0), where ΔG = G2 – G1.
Here, G1 represents the Gibbs free energy of the separated solute and solvent, and G2 represents that of the homogeneous solution.
If ΔG > 0, dissolution is non-spontaneous, indicating poor solubility.
If ΔG = 0, the system attains a dynamic dissolution–precipitation equilibrium.
This thermodynamic criterion determines the spontaneity of dissolution.
The dissolution process primarily involves two steps: (i) dissociation of the solute lattice and (ii) solvation of the dissociated ions.
(i) Lattice dissociation.
